prize_parts.citation: for establishing the physical principles of long-range electron transfer through proteins

statement.case_for: B054 is the one shortlisted candidacy that rests on a single, quantitatively tested mechanistic discovery in biological chemistry. Gray and Winkler, using ruthenium-modified proteins with defined donor-acceptor distances, showed how rate depends on distance, driving force, reorganization energy and the intervening medium, and how multistep hopping extends the reach of electron transfer. That framework is how redox enzymes and respiratory and photosynthetic chains are now analysed. It is physical chemistry stated in physical terms and tested by kinetics, not a methods catalogue. The credit is compact: two named people, well within the three-laureate limit. The work is about forty years old, independently confirmed and in the textbooks, so timing is not an issue. My own field (electron and proton transfer in cytochrome c oxidase) draws heavily on this framework, which is why I can judge its depth, and why my view needs to be tested against colleagues who do not share my background.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that this candidacy has almost no opening support. It is first on my ballot only, and a prize needs five of eight votes. Attribution is also not as clean as the two-name credit suggests: the theoretical foundation (Marcus, Hopfield, Jortner) and the tunneling-pathway and protein-engineering contributions of Beratan, Onuchic, Dutton and Moser are outside the supplied credit. Marcus has already been recognised for electron-transfer theory (1992), so the committee may regard protein electron transfer as an application of an honoured theory. A careful reading of the expert reports would have to show that Gray and Winkler established something that experiment had not already shown, and that is the point I cannot settle from the shortlist alone.

responses.point: Aqvist ranks Car-Parrinello molecular dynamics first: a 1985 paper by exactly two authors, unambiguous priority, four decades of independent use, and a simple idea that changed how liquids, solutions and proton transfer are simulated.
responses.response: I agree that B007 has the cleanest attribution on the shortlist, and that clean priority matters when the limit is three laureates. It is also close to my own interests, since first-principles simulation of proton transfer in water is the natural counterpart of the experiments on my side of the field. My qualification is about novelty of recognition. Computational chemistry was honoured in 2013 for multiscale models and in 2024 for structure prediction, and Parrinello's later contributions (metadynamics, machine-learned potentials) raise the question whether the prize should honour a single 1985 paper or a larger body of work. I would not oppose B007 on merit, and I list it as my first alternative. I do not regard it as a stronger case than B054, because B054 links a physical principle directly to measured kinetics in biological molecules.

responses.point: Linke ranks base editing first and argues that Liu, Komor and Gaudelli form a defensible trio: a clear principle, a new chemical capability on the genome, extensive replication and the first patients treated.
responses.response: I agree that base editing is a chemically inventive and consequential idea, and that Liu is the intellectual driver. I disagree on two points. First, the 2020 prize for CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing is a recent precedent, and a base-editing prize would be read as a follow-on to it, with the parallel deaminase-Cas9 work of Nishida and Kondo further muddying priority. Second, I would not give prize status to trainees alongside Liu simply because the trio fits the limit of three. The clinical record is only starting to accumulate, and long-term safety and off-target deamination are still open. I would keep B021 under observation and not decide it this year. I do not rank it above the more mature candidacies.

responses.point: Chabes ranks Balasubramanian and Klenerman first: sequencing by synthesis with reversible terminators turned polymerase chemistry into a massively parallel readout, is exceptionally mature, and is arguably overdue.
responses.response: I think this is the strongest of the biotechnology candidacies, and the chemistry of reversible terminators is a genuine, original invention, which is why B055 is my second alternative. My concern is attribution, which is where a committee earns its caution. Rothberg (454 pyrosequencing), Mayer (clonal clustering) and Ju (terminator chemistry) all have credible priority claims, and Chabes treats them as parallel contributions whereas I would want the expert report to show exactly where the decisive step lies. Without a clean answer, a two-person prize risks being challenged as incomplete. I also want to know whether the committee values a technology that transformed biology as the same thing as a chemical discovery. That is a question of how we read the will, and it should be answered explicitly before we vote.

responses.point: Sparr ranks biomolecular phase separation first, framing condensates as a physical-chemical problem of phase behaviour and multivalency, with Hyman, Brangwynne and Rosen as the core trio.
responses.response: As a physical-chemistry argument I find this appealing, and it is the kind of concept I want mechanisms to be expressed in. My reservation is the same as the one Linke raised in his opening ballot: the in-vivo evidence is still contested. We do not yet know which cellular assemblies are truly liquid-liquid phase separated, and quantitative links from the physical state to cellular function are thinner than the textbook version suggests. A principle that is still being tested in its main application is less mature than the kinetics of electron transfer. I would support B063 in several years, if the physiological case firms up, but I do not think it is ready this year.

responses.point: Zou ranks template-directed mesoporous silica first, as a clear synthetic concept that opened a new class of porous solids and is overdue after three decades of independent use.
responses.response: I agree with the maturity argument and I respect the structural-chemistry reasoning. I note that Zou is a Stockholm University colleague, and that this does not affect my reading of the case. My difficulty is that the credit is spread across six names, and the committee would have to choose between the Mobil group, the independent Japanese FSM-16 work, and the later SBA and KIT contributions of Zhao, Stucky and Ryoo. A three-person cut here is more arbitrary than for B054, and there is a risk that it leaves out someone whose work is at least as decisive. If Zou can identify the three people whose individual contributions are not replaceable, I would take the proposal seriously.

uncertainties: Whether the expert report places Gray and Winkler's experiments as an independent discovery or as a verification of Marcus-type theory already honoured in 1992.
How much credit the omitted theory and protein-engineering contributions (Beratan, Onuchic, Dutton, Moser) should carry relative to the two named experimentalists.
Whether a sufficiently large bloc of members will accept a biophysical-chemistry prize when my candidacy has no other first-place support.
Whether the committee treats enabling analytical or sequencing technologies as chemical discoveries in the sense of the will, which would affect B055 and B021.
statement.conflict_note: No personal or institutional connection to any shortlisted candidate is apparent from my profile. I note two things for transparency. My research field (electron and proton transfer in respiratory enzymes) is scientifically adjacent to B054, which gives me expertise but also a possible bias in its favour. I am also a Stockholm University colleague of Xiaodong Zou, whose first-ranked candidacy is B043, and I have no stake in that case. None of this requires recusal in my view, but the committee should be aware of it.
